o: The apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope.
Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge.
Gives a glorious view of Christ.
And sets out his own character, as the apostle of the Gentiles.
bg: colossians, epistle to the

Was written by Paul at Rome during his first imprisonment there (Acts 28:16, 30), probably in the spring of A.D. 57, or, as some think, 62, and soon after he had written his Epistle to the Ephesians. Like some of his other epistles (e.g., those to Corinth), this seems to have been written in consequence of information which had somehow been conveyed to him of the internal state of the church there
Colosse
more properly Colos'sae, was a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, in the upper part of the basin of the Maeander, on the Lycus. Hierapolis and Laodicea were in its immediate neighborhood.
Paul

After a short rest at Antioch, Paul said to Barnabas: "Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do." Mark proposed again to accompany them; but Paul refused to allow him to go.
Epaphras
Lovely, spoken of by Paul (Col. 1:7; 4:12) as "his dear fellow-servant," and "a faithful minister of Christ." He was thus evidently with him at Rome when he wrote to the Colossians.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope (vv. 1–8); Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge (vv. 9–14); Gives a glorious view of Christ (vv. 15–23); And sets out his own character, as the apostle of the Gentiles (vv. 24–29). People named: Paul, Timotheus, Epaphras. Places: Colosse.
ch.mh: All true Christians are brethren one to another.
q: Read verses 1–8 (The apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–14 (Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge), what do you learn about the church and fellowship?
Verse 13 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Ephesians 5:8. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Paul’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Colossians?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We must be faithful to death, through all trials, that we may receive the crown of life, and obtain the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

o: The apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers.
He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ.
Against worshipping angels; and against legal ordinances.

Laodicea

The city of this name mentioned in Scripture lay on the confines of Phrygia and Lydia, about 40 miles east of Ephesus (Rev. 3:14), on the banks of the Lycus. It was originally called Diospolis and then Rhoas, but afterwards Laodicea, from Laodice, the wife of Antiochus II., king of Syria, who rebuilt it.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers (vv. 1–7); He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ (vv. 8–17); Against worshipping angels; and against legal ordinances (vv. 18–23). Places: Laodicea.
ch.mh: The soul prospers when we have clear knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus.
q: Read verses 1–7 (The apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–17 (He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ), what do you learn about wisdom?
Verse 8 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 Timothy 6:20. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of faith and trust in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Colossians?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: What the Lord has left indifferent, let us regard as such, and leave others to the like freedom; and remembering the passing nature of earthly things, let us seek to glorify God in the use of them.
ch.a: Before a decision this week, pause and ask what this chapter would counsel.

Jew
(a man of Judea). This name was properly applied to a member of the kingdom of Judah after the separation of the ten tribes.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The Colossians exhorted to be heavenly-minded; (vv. 1–4); to mortify all corrupt affections; (vv. 5–11); to live in mutual love, forbearance, and forgiveness; (vv. 12–17); and to practise the duties of wives and husbands, children, parents, and servants (vv. 18–25). People named: Jew.
ch.mh: As Christians are freed from the ceremonial law, they must walk the more closely with God in gospel obedience.
q: Read verses 1–4 (The Colossians exhorted to be heavenly-minded;). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?

Verse 16 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 119:11. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jew’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of the church and fellowship in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Colossians?

ch.aq: We must never separate the privileges and duties of the gospel.
ch.a: Write down three things this chapter shows about God and thank Him for each.

o: Masters to do their duty towards servants.
Persons of all ranks to persevere in prayer, and Christian prudence.
The apostle refers to others for an account of his affairs.
Sends greetings; and concludes with a blessing.
bg: colossians, epistle to the

Was written by Paul at Rome during his first imprisonment there (Acts 28:16, 30), probably in the spring of A.D. 57, or, as some think, 62, and soon after he had written his Epistle to the Ephesians. Like some of his other epistles (e.g., those to Corinth), this seems to have been written in consequence of information which had somehow been conveyed to him of the internal state of the church there
Laodicea

The city of this name mentioned in Scripture lay on the confines of Phrygia and Lydia, about 40 miles east of Ephesus (Rev. 3:14), on the banks of the Lycus. It was originally called Diospolis and then Rhoas, but afterwards Laodicea, from Laodice, the wife of Antiochus II., king of Syria, who rebuilt it.
Hierapolis
Sacred city, a city of Phrygia, where was a Christian church under the care of Epaphras (Col. 4:12, 13). This church was founded at the same time as that of Colosse.
Tychicus

Chance, an Asiatic Christian, a "faithful minister in the Lord" (Eph. 6:21, 22), who, with Trophimus, accompanied Paul on a part of his journey from Macedonia to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). He is alluded to also in Col. 4:7, Titus 3:12, and 2 Tim. 4:12 as having been with Paul at Rome, whence he sent him to Ephesus, probably for the purpose of building up and encouraging the church there.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Masters to do their duty towards servants (vv. 1); Persons of all ranks to persevere in prayer, and Christian prudence (vv. 2–6); The apostle refers to others for an account of his affairs (vv. 7–9); Sends greetings; and concludes with a blessing (vv. 10–18). People named: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Marcus, Barnabas, Justus. Places: Laodicea, Hierapolis.
ch.mh: The apostle proceeds with the duty of masters to their servants.
q: Read verses 1 (Masters to do their duty towards servants). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 2–6 (Persons of all ranks to persevere in prayer, and Christian prudence), what do you learn about the church and fellowship?
Verse 6 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Ephesians 4:29. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Tychicus’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of prayer in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Colossians?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
